commands.speak: Now that we have seen whose values count, take one group of people and ask about the same state three ways.
On a visual analogue scale, they simply mark the state on a line from dead to full health, like a thermometer.
In a time trade-off, they give up years of life to live the rest in full health.
In a standard gamble, they accept a risk of death for a chance at full health.
For the same state, the numbers usually fall in the same order: the gamble highest, the trade-off next, the scale lowest.
Our 0.5 is a trade-off value; the scale might say 0.4, the gamble 0.6 — illustrative numbers.
The gamble comes out high because most people dislike risk: facing a chance of death, they cling to the state they know.
The trade-off has its own pull: distant years feel worth less, so people give more of them up, which pulls the weight down.
The scale asks for no sacrifice at all: it records a feeling about the state, not a choice.
None of the three is simply right; each builds its own assumption about risk and time into the weight.
Payers answer by fixing one method in advance — NICE uses EQ-5D values from time trade-off — so every drug is measured with the same ruler.
So a weight is not a fact about the state; it is the state seen through a method.

quiz.question: A state is valued at 0.8 by standard gamble. Valued by time trade-off, the same people would most likely give it…
quiz.right: A lower weight: the gamble's number is pushed up by dislike of risk, and the trade-off usually lands below it.
quiz.wrong: Think about what dislike of risk does to the gamble's number.
